hypothesis: The near-tie band `band = 1e-3 * (span + 1.0)` mixes a relative unit (span) with an absolute length unit (1.0), so the width of the band is not equivariant under a change of the coordinate scale; the band should therefore dominate the rule when the instance is shrunk and vanish when it is enlarged.
findings: Scale non-equivariance is real and monotone in the scale factor (+48% at 1e-2, +207% at 1e-3).
The branch rate tracks the mechanism prediction 1.33% -> 64.3% -> 82.7% -> 0%.
A purely relative band restores equivariance (0.39% spread) but costs 1.92% at the nominal scale, so the absolute +1.0 is not a pure defect: on the unit square it lands on a useful width.
The construct path is almost entirely different after shrinking (3.33% per-decision agreement), so the failure is structural rather than a small perturbation.
guidance: Replace the additive constant with a scale-free gate: keep the firing width that is useful on the nominal unit square, but define it relative to the realized score span (for example a fixed multiple of the top-2 base gap, or a relative band whose coefficient is calibrated so that the nominal firing rate stays near 1-2%). Do not simply divide by span with the same 1e-3 coefficient.

verification.why: Mechanism confirmed, naive remedy rejected by its own measurement; the guidance keeps the validated part and discards the refuted part.
verification.next_test: Generate the calibrated relative-band variant and evaluate it on dev_suite before spending provider budget.

target_rule: algorithm portfolio {nn, savings, dd_load, radial} on three CVRP regimes
hypothesis: No single constructive rule dominates across instance regimes, and the regime can be detected from pre-solve features, so an instance-level selector can recover part of the oracle gap.
findings: Complementarity is real but modest: the oracle saves 4.23% over the best fixed rule.
The best fixed rule changes with the regime (dd_load / savings / radial), so the portfolio is not redundant.
Within-pool feature regression beats the fixed choice by 1.15pp (3.07% vs 4.23% gap).
No cross-regime transfer: leave-one-regime-out is 6.57%, worse than fixing one algorithm, so a universal selector cannot be claimed.
1-NN on the same features is worse than the fixed choice (5.11%), which rules out 'any learner works'.
guidance: Write the regime dependence into the rule instead of assuming one trade-off: make the tie-break branch selectable by detectable structure (cluster tendency, depot eccentricity, capacity ratio) rather than by a single global coefficient, and keep a fixed fallback for regimes the rule cannot classify.

verification.why: Complementarity and regime dependence are measured on 36 deterministic instances with the real evaluator; the selector result is reported as within-pool only.
verification.next_test: Regenerate with the regime-conditional branch as a research_finding and check whether EoH can realize it inside one rule; extend the testbed to 100/200 customers.
